The anti-vortex film cooling concept proposes adding two branched holes from each primary hole to produce a vorticity counter to the detrimental kidney vortices.
The computational study considered blowing ratios of 1.0 and 2.0, and density ratios of 1.0 and 2.0, to represent a range of engine-relevant conditions.
The Reynolds number based on hole diameter was 11,300 in the simulations.

The 'adjacent' anti-vortex design, where the side holes exit adjacent to the main jet, showed improved film cooling effectiveness compared to the baseline round holes and the 'upstream' anti-vortex design.
The computational grid sensitivity study showed relatively small differences, typically less than 10%, between the fine grid (~2.5 million cells) and coarse grid (~300,000 cells) results.

The adjacent anti-vortex design required nearly the same plenum pressure as the baseline round holes to achieve the target blowing ratios, while the upstream anti-vortex design showed a moderate reduction in the required plenum pressure.

The anti-vortex concept may offer benefits for turbine blades subject to deposition and plugging of the film cooling holes, as the side holes provide an alternate path for the coolant to exit the blade.
The anti-vortex design requires only easily machinable round holes, unlike shaped film cooling holes which can be more expensive to manufacture.
The anti-vortex design does not increase the coolant flow rate for a given plenum pressure like adding a second row of holes would.
The computational results showed the anti-vortex design effectively countered the detrimental kidney vortices present in the baseline round hole configuration.
The modified 'adjacent' anti-vortex design showed the best performance, with a flatter, more attached coolant jet at the downstream locations studied.
The side holes in the anti-vortex design produce a vorticity that is counter to the detrimental kidney vortices generated by the main jet.
The key geometric parameters studied were the side hole diameter (50% of main hole), spanwise pitch (3 hole diameters), and side hole angle.

Two variants of the anti-vortex design were studied: an 'upstream' design where the side holes emerged upstream of the main jet, and an 'adjacent' design where the side holes exited adjacent to the main jet.
The computational results confirmed the experimental findings that the 'adjacent' anti-vortex design provides the best film cooling performance.
